data.name: server.instructions
data.value:
Kontext is your long-term memory, spoken in six verbs: - Retain (store something worth remembering) - Recall (search by meaning) - Reclaim (fetch by id) - Recollect (browse by type/tag) - Reflect (synthesize higher-level memories from what's there)
Recall before you guess — re-deriving something you already learned is the expensive path. Retain the moment you learn something durable, written to stand on its own. To correct a memory, retain the correction with supersedes. Reflect periodically, when observations pile up — not on every turn.

data.name: tool.recall
data.value: Search your memory by MEANING — not reclaim (that's by id), not recollect (that's by type/tag, no ranking). Reach for this before you act on something you might already know: at the start of a task, when a name, decision, error, file, or preference comes up that you may have seen before, or any time you'd otherwise guess. Recalling is cheap; re-deriving something you already learned — or silently contradicting a past decision — is not. Results come back ranked best-first: treat the order as the system's confidence and each memory's type as how far to trust it (a firsthand OBSERVATION outranks HEARSAY picked up in conversation). Only what is currently true surfaces — superseded and superseded memories never do. Side effect worth knowing: recalling a memory keeps it salient (refreshes its recency clock), so the things you actually use stay near the top over time. Recall freely.

data.name: tool.recall.param.options
data.value: Optional knobs — limit, minimum score, tag pre-filter, include-full. Null ⇒ server defaults.

data.name: tool.recall.param.query
data.value: What you are trying to remember, in natural language — phrase it like a question to a colleague ("what did we decide about the checkpoint format?"), not keywords.

data.name: tool.reclaim
data.value: Fetch exact memories by id — not recall (that's by meaning), not recollect (that's by type/tag). Use it for progressive disclosure: when an earlier result (a recall hit, a reflection) handed you only ids and you now want the complete folded records, provenance (evidence, reasoning) included. Not a search and no ranking — you get exactly the ids you asked for, including superseded records (you asked by id, so they are not hidden here). Ids that don't exist are simply absent from the result, never an error — diff the returned ids against what you asked for to see which missed. Like recall, reclaiming refreshes the recency clock of the memories it returns.

data.name: tool.recollect
data.value: Browse your memories by structure, not relevance — not recall (that ranks by meaning), not reclaim (that's by id). Use it to enumerate or gather a filtered set — "all my PLANs tagged project::engram", "everything I retained this week" — where you want a list, not a ranked answer to a question. The types filter is any-of (empty = any type); all supplied tags must be present. still surfaces them). Ordered by sort (default: newest-retained first); reverse with direction. Read-only.

data.name: tool.reflect
data.value: Step back and synthesize. This recalls broadly over the store and writes higher-level, DERIVED memories from what it finds — a FACT, PROCEDURE, PROFILE, SUMMARY, or PLAN that cites the memories it rests on — and may supersede or supersede the ones the new insight subsumes. Reflection is the operation that produces derived memories; there is no "reflection" memory type. Reach for it periodically, when a pile of observations wants to become a durable conclusion — not on every turn. Writes new memories and is destructive (may supersede); long-running — expect it to complete asynchronously rather than return instantly. Not idempotent. Returns the ids it synthesized, and superseded.

data.name: tool.reflect.param.options
data.value: Optional correlation id and tag scoping. Null ⇒ the server assigns an id and reflects over everything.

data.name: tool.retain
data.value:
Store something worth remembering — a decision and its reasoning, an error and its fix, a user preference, a durable fact, a question you could not answer. Reach for it the moment you learn something you'd want back later, and write each memory so it stands on its own: a reader months from now, with no other context, should understand it. Set the memory type honestly — it is the trust axis, so don't dress an unchecked claim up as a Fact — set importance by how much it matters, cite what the memory rests on in evidence, put the argument in reasoning, and list any memories it replaces in supersedes (the old ones stay readable, marked superseded; there is no separate supersede call).
YOU DO NOT SUPPLY IDS. The server mints every id and returns them positionally: result[i] is the memory you sent at position i, always, same length, same order. So you cannot cite a memory you are sending in this same call — retain the sources first, then retain the memory that cites them. If that second call fails you are left with valid standalone memories, which is harmless.
EVERY RETAIN REPORTS ITS NEIGHBOURS. There is no flag: the server always searches for the closest LIVE memories to each one you store and returns them in related, nearest first. It does not merge, block, or deduplicate anything — it reports, YOU decide. Reading related is part of making this call, not a courtesy. When a neighbour matches what you just stored: if you brought NEW SUPPORT (a second encounter, a different source), retain a successor with supersedes on it, carrying the union of its citations and yours — re-encountering a belief is corroboration and worth recording; if you
Additive and always creates: retaining the same content twice creates two memories, which is exactly why you must act on related. Returns one result per memory, in order, with its server-assigned id and its neighbours.

data.name: tool.retain.param.memories
data.value: One or more memories to store — each written to stand on its own.

data.name: tool.reclaim.param.ids
data.value: The exact memory ids to fetch back.

data.name: tool.recollect.param.options
data.value: The filters and ordering — types (any-of), tags (all-of), limit, sort, direction.

data.name: tool.reflect.param.query
data.value: What to reflect on, in natural language — the theme to synthesize over.

data.name: type.Evidence
data.value:
One cited source. Exactly one arm is set: a memory, a KurrentDB log record, a location in git, or text on the web. Provenance on a raw memory ("where I saw this") and support on a derived one — a memory counts as DERIVED only when it cites at least one MEMORY; citing files or pages means you looked something up firsthand and leaves it raw.
Cite only what is OUTSIDE the memory. A check you ran yourself — a search, a build, a test run — is not a source: if it matters, say so in content or reasoning. A search result in particular is not evidence; cite the thing it found, and put "nothing else does this" in reasoning where a reader can discount it.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToMemory
data.value: A citation of another memory. The only arm that makes this memory derived.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToMemory.memory
data.value: The cited memory.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToRecord
data.value: A citation of a KurrentDB log record.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToRecord.record
data.value: The cited KurrentDB log record.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToGit
data.value: A citation of a location in a git repository.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToGit.git
data.value: The cited source location.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToWeb
data.value: A citation of text on the web.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToWeb.web
data.value: The cited page, with the passages that made it worth citing.

data.name: type.GitRef
data.value: A location in a git repository. The ANCHOR is the commit: without it the citation rots silently as the file moves. Prefer a symbol over a line range — a symbol survives a refactor, a line number rots within days. Reach for lines only where there is no symbol to name (an XML element, a config entry, a data file).

data.name: type.GitRef.repo
data.value: owner/name. Leave unset for the repository the memory is being retained from.

data.name: type.GitRef.commit
data.value: The anchor — the revision this citation was true at.

data.name: type.GitRef.branch
data.value: Advisory only: a branch moves, so it anchors nothing.

data.name: type.GitRef.path
data.value: Repo-relative path.

data.name: type.GitRef.symbol
data.value: The type or member cited. Preferred over lines — it survives line drift.

data.name: type.GitRef.lineStart
data.value: Fallback for files with no symbol to name.

data.name: type.GitRef.lineEnd
data.value: Fallback for files with no symbol to name.

data.name: type.GitRef.excerpt
data.value: Optional, 20..1000 characters. Expected when the repo is NOT ours: a third-party repository can go private or vanish, and then the commit resolves to nothing. Our own history is immutable, so an excerpt there is redundant.

data.name: type.WebRef
data.value: A pointer to TEXT on the web — an article, a documentation page, a specification, a post. NOT a file, PDF, archive, or binary target. The ANCHOR is the excerpts, not the URI and not the timestamp: pages are deleted, rewritten, paywalled and moved, and when that happens the excerpt is the only surviving evidence.

data.name: type.WebRef.uri
data.value: The page's address.

data.name: type.WebRef.title
data.value: The page's title, if it has one.

data.name: type.WebRef.excerpts
data.value: Required: 1..5 passages, each 20..1000 characters — the sentences you would quote if asked "where does it say that?". A web citation without one is a bookmark, not a citation, and is rejected. Keep each a passage, not a page: if you need six, you are summarizing the source, and that is a memory of its own.

data.name: type.WebRef.retrievedAt
data.value: When the excerpts were taken — metadata about the excerpt, not the anchor.

data.name: type.LeanMemory
data.value: The lean recall projection: enough to use a memory and judge it, without the provenance trail (evidence, reasoning). For those, request the full body or reclaim by id.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.content
data.value: The memory text.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.importance
data.value: Its salience level.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.memoryId
data.value: Reclaim by this id for the full record.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.memoryType
data.value: The trust axis — the record's cognitive type.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.retainedAt
data.value: When the memory was retained — age, for context.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.tags
data.value: Labels carried on the memory.

data.name: type.Memory
data.value: A memory's intrinsic content — the write/command shape passed to retain. The read path returns the folded stored memory; the two shapes are deliberately separate so the write and read models evolve independently.

data.name: type.Memory.content
data.value: The memory's textual content.

data.name: type.Memory.evidence
data.value: The sources this memory cites, in citation order. Empty is normal and costs nothing beyond the flat per-type trust weight — most durable facts are asserted directly and carry no citation at all. A HEARSAY memory must carry none and is REJECTED if it does: verify the claim and retain a Fact that supersedes it.

data.name: type.Memory.reasoning
data.value: Why this record exists in this shape. Two obligations, in order: (1) why the claim is TRUE — the derivation from the cited sources to the conclusion, present when you synthesized it, absent when it is firsthand or directly asserted; (2) why it is FILED THIS WAY — only when the type or importance was a judgment call at a contested boundary (Hearsay vs Observation, Preference vs Fact, OpenQuestion vs Hearsay). Skip (2) when the classification was obvious. Most memories need only (1), or neither. Kept out of content and out of the recall embedding: the embedding indexes the memory's own claim, never the argument for it.

data.name: type.Memory.importance
data.value: The agent's salience rating — how much this memory matters. Higher importance keeps it retrievable longer as recency fades; it does not change the decay rate. Default: Normal.

data.name: type.Memory.supersedes
data.value: Memory ids this memory supersedes (replaces). The superseded ones stay readable, marked superseded. Set at retain — there is no separate supersede operation.

data.name: type.Memory.tags
data.value: Scoped or bare labels.

data.name: type.Memory.type
data.value: The record's cognitive type — Kontext's trust axis (replaces an explicit confidence field).

data.name: type.Memory.validity
data.value: The world-time span the content refers to (perceived from the text); a point event sets start == end. Null when the text implies none.

data.name: type.MemoryImportance
data.value:
The agent's salience rating, set at retain. An additive term in ranking, not a decay control: higher importance keeps a memory's score up as recency fades, so it stays retrievable longer — it does not change the decay rate. A coarse bucket by design.
Values: - Unspecified: Not set — treated as Normal. - Low: Incidental — fine to let it fade. - Normal: The default. - High: Decisions, fixes, preferences worth keeping. - Critical: Top salience — architectural calls, hard-won lessons.

data.name: type.MemoryRef
data.value: A pointer to another memory that supports this one.

data.name: type.MemoryRef.id
data.value: The cited memory id.

data.name: type.MemoryRef.position
data.value: Its position in the log (exact, replayable).

data.name: type.MemoryType
data.value:
What a memory is — Kontext's trust axis. Whether a memory is firsthand or derived is not a type: it is visible in its evidence (cites at least one MEMORY ⇒ derived, inheriting the certainty of those memories; anything else ⇒ firsthand or asserted). There is deliberately no "reflection" type — reflection is the process that produces the derived types.
THE LIFECYCLE TEST, which decides episodic vs durable: "does TIME ALONE make this irrelevant, or does something have to HAPPEN?" Time alone ⇒ episodic, it decays (Observation, Hearsay, OpenQuestion). Something must happen ⇒ durable, never decayed, superseded when the world changes (Fact, Preference, UserProfile, Summary). Persistence is not a claim of eternal truth — it means only that decay would be the WRONG reason to lose it.
Values: - Unspecified: Default / not set. - Observation: A perceived EVENT — "what happened". Firsthand, so the highest trust. Episodic (decays). The word names the SHAPE OF THE CLAIM, not the act of observing: reading a file is an act of observation, but what you learn from it is usually a standing state, and that is a Fact. "The build failed at 15:04" is an Observation; "the bus dispatches parent handlers first" is a Fact. - Hearsay: An UNVERIFIED CLAIM — someone asserts this is true and you have not checked. Naturally low-trust, kept unverified so a fabricated "fact" injected into you cannot launder itself into truth (the "memory-hacking" guard). Episodic. Defined by verification status, not origin: a claim from a blog post, a stale code comment, or a colleague all land here. When a conversation gives you both readings, ask "is this useful because it WAS SAID, or because of WHAT WAS SAID?" — the saying is an Observation, the content is Hearsay, and usually you want the content. Carries NO evidence: citing a memory would make it a derived inference, and citing a source would mean you verified it. To promote it, verify and retain a Fact that supersedes it. - Fact: A durable truth about the world, a system, or a project — a coding standard, a how-to, a milestone, a property of the code. A STANDING STATE, not an event. Persists; superseded, never decayed. Scope is irrelevant to the type: "humans need air" and "this project runs tests only via test-runner.cs" are the same kind of record — scope is what tags are for. EVIDENCE IS NOT WHAT MAKES A FACT: most carry none, and missing evidence costs certainty, not validity. - UserProfile: Identity and role of a principal — who they are, deliberately small. Always loaded for that principal, so only identity-grade facts belong here. - Preference: A personal taste binding only its principal ("I prefer tabs"). Persists, superseded freely as taste drifts, earned by relevance — never always-loaded. A preference binding a team/project is a standard: a Fact at that scope, not a Preference. - Summary: A consolidation of other memories — a recap, digest, or index. Always derived (cites its sources as evidence), so its certainty is inherited from them. Persists, refreshed as those sources change. - OpenQuestion: A KNOWN GAP — something unresolved that still needs an answer. The only NON-ASSERTIVE type: it carries no proposition, so it has no truth value, cannot be corroborated or contradicted, and certainty is meaningless for it. That is what earns it a place; every other type is a claim. Episodic, and decay IS the moot mechanism — a question nobody recalls fades without ceremony, so no anti-fact is ever needed. Enumerate them with recollect (which does not rank, so decay never hides one from that path); that list is your work queue. It terminates by being ANSWERED: retain the answering Fact with supersedes on it. Never citable as evidence — a claim cannot rest on a question. Versus Hearsay: hearsay is a LOW-CONFIDENCE ANSWER, an open question is the ABSENCE of one, and both can be live at once.
There is no Procedure type (a how-to is a Fact) and no Plan type (a stated intention is an unverified claim about the future — Hearsay; it decays when stale).

data.name: type.RecallOptions
data.value: The optional knobs for a recall — the query itself is a direct parameter.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.includeFull
data.value: When true, each hit carries the complete folded record instead of the lean projection. Default false: lean hits, easier on your context.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.limit
data.value: How many memories to return after ranking. Ask for a handful (5–10); asking for many more mostly dilutes the top results.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.minScore
data.value: Drop anything the server scores below this cutoff — raise it when you only want strong matches, leave it at 0 to see everything that ranked.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.queryId
data.value: Optional correlation id for this recall; null ⇒ the server assigns one. Keep it to tie later feedback or inspection back to this exact query.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.tags
data.value: Optional pre-filter: only memories carrying these tags are considered. Use it only when you already know the dimension to narrow to; empty ⇒ search everything.

data.name: type.RecallResult
data.value: Result of a recall — hits ranked best-first.

data.name: type.RecallResult.memories
data.value: The recall hits, ranked best-first.

data.name: type.RecallResult.queryId
data.value: Echoes the recall's query id (assigned by the server if it was left empty).

data.name: type.RecalledMemory
data.value: One recall hit — a ranking score plus the memory, lean by default or the full folded record when include-full was set. Exactly one body arm is set.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Full
data.value: The complete folded record (as reclaim returns) — present when include-full was set.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Full.memory
data.value: The complete folded record of the hit.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Lean
data.value: The default lean projection — enough to use and trust a hit.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Lean.memory
data.value: The lean projection of the hit.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory.score
data.value: Final ranking score (base × certainty); higher = stronger match. A low top score means nothing matched well.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions
data.value: The filters and ordering for a recollect — browse by structure (type/tags), not relevance. Recollect has no payload, so every input lives here.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.direction
data.value: Sort direction. Default: descending.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.limit
data.value: Max memories to return. With a limit, the sort decides which slice you get.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.sort
data.value: How to order results. Default: newest-retained first. Reach for Importance when you want the top-N significant memories rather than the most recent.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.tags
data.value: Optional filter: only memories carrying ALL of these tags (empty ⇒ no tag filter).

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.types
data.value: Optional filter: any-of these types (empty ⇒ any type).

data.name: type.RecollectSort
data.value:
The dimension a recollect orders its results by (there is no relevance here — that's recall).
Values: - Unspecified: Not set — defaults to RetainedAt. - RetainedAt: When the memory was recorded — chronological. The default. - LastAccessedAt: The recency clock — surfaces what has been salient (recalled) lately. - Importance: The agent's salience rating — surfaces the significant ones. Pairs well with a limit: the top-N important memories rather than arbitrary ones.

data.name: type.RecordRef
data.value: A pointer to a KurrentDB log record that supports this memory.

data.name: type.RecordRef.id
data.value: The record's id.

data.name: type.RecordRef.position
data.value: Its position in the log (exact, replayable).

data.name: type.ReflectOptions
data.value: The optional knobs for a reflect pass — the theme (query) is a direct parameter.

data.name: type.ReflectOptions.queryId
data.value: Optional correlation id for this reflection; null ⇒ the server assigns one.

data.name: type.ReflectOptions.tags
data.value: Scope the reflection to memories carrying these tags; empty ⇒ range over all.

data.name: type.ReflectResult
data.value: Result of a reflect pass: the ids it synthesized, and superseded.

data.name: type.ReflectResult.queryId
data.value: Correlates to the reflect call — supplied on the request, or server-assigned.

data.name: type.ReflectResult.supersededMemoryIds
data.value: Ids of memories superseded.

data.name: type.ReflectResult.synthesizedMemoryIds
data.value: Ids of memories synthesized.

data.name: type.RelatedMemory
data.value: A pre-existing memory that looks related to a just-stored one.

data.name: type.RelatedMemory.memory
data.value: The related, pre-existing memory.

data.name: type.RelatedMemory.similarity
data.value: Embedding cosine, ~0..1 (higher = more alike).

data.name: type.RetainResult
data.value: Result of a retain — one outcome per input memory, in the same order.

data.name: type.RetainResult.results
data.value: One result per input memory, in order.

data.name: type.RetainedMemory
data.value: The outcome for a single stored memory.

data.name: type.RetainedMemory.memoryId
data.value: The stored memory's id. Retain always stores; the related list never blocks it.

data.name: type.RetainedMemory.related
data.value: Advisory, populated only when retain was asked to reconcile: existing memories this one looks to duplicate or contradict, nearest first.

data.name: type.SortDirection
data.value:
Sort direction for a recollect listing.
Values: - Unspecified: Not set — defaults to Descending. - Descending: High → low: newest / most-important / most-recently-accessed first. - Ascending: Low → high: oldest / least first.

data.name: type.StoredMemory
data.value: The complete, folded read model of a single memory — every lifecycle event applied. Self-contained, for inspection and direct fetch (reclaim/recollect), not for ranked retrieval. Deliberately separate from the memory command shape so read and write models evolve independently.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.content
data.value: The memory's textual content.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.reasoning
data.value: Why the claim is true and, when it was a judgment call, why it is filed this way.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.evidence
data.value: What this memory rests on: cited sources and the reasoning tying them to it. Empty for a raw observation.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.importance
data.value: The salience level set at retain (higher keeps it retrievable longer as recency fades).

data.name: type.StoredMemory.lastAccessedAt
data.value: When the memory was last accessed — the recency clock, advanced by each recall. Null if never accessed.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.memoryId
data.value: Unique identifier of the memory.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.memoryType
data.value: The record's cognitive type — Kontext's trust axis.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.retainedAt
data.value: When the memory was retained.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.supersededAt
data.value: When a newer memory superseded this one, if any.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.supersededBy
data.value: The memory that superseded this one; set only when superseded-at is set.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.supersedes
data.value: Memory ids this memory supersedes (replaces).

data.name: type.StoredMemory.tags
data.value: Scoped or bare labels.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.validity
data.value: The world-time span the content refers to (perceived from the text).

data.name: type.Tag
data.value: An agent-agnostic filter label with an optional scope (namespace). Scoped tags let you filter on a typed dimension (e.g. project:kurrentdb) without a contract change per dimension, and the same scope can repeat on one memory. Both value and scope are sanitized to lower kebab-case, so tags are canonical.

data.name: type.Tag.scope
data.value: Optional namespace — lower kebab-case; empty ⇒ bare tag.

data.name: type.Tag.value
data.value: The label — lower kebab-case.

data.name: type.TemporalContext
type.TemporalContext.from
data.value: Start of the state, or the moment of a point event.

data.name: type.TemporalContext.to
data.value: End of the interval; null ⇒ ongoing / open-ended.
